translations.text: Let every mouth open today in blessing, and let every utterance sing the praises of the Word of God who has shone forth from heaven. Let every tongue speak, let every soul rejoice, let the whole earth sing:
For today words of light illumine the sons of light. Let earthly things join in harmony with heavenly things; let the visible things in the world sing with the powers above the world:
For since the truth has appeared and the heavenly King has come, everyone should gather together in a common confession of the Lord of all.
Christ’s coming is a blessing to the whole inhabited earth. Christ’s coming is the liberation of the whole world.
Christ is praised in song, and the world is sanctified.
Christ is proclaimed, and every soul is clothed in heavenly love. The evidence of things bears witness to my words.
Behold this godly ordering of the church; behold the unquenchable heavenly lamp; behold bodily nature striving to match the service of angels. The fathers, being of the earth,
and living on the earth, and nourished from the earth,
rival the heavenly beings: for such is the church of God.
It lives on earth, yet has the order of heavenly things. What is the work of the angels in heaven? To serve God.
What is the work of the holy ones on earth? To sing God’s praises. Their dignity, therefore, is also equal in honor.
For this reason blessed David, striking his spiritual harp and proclaiming salvation through the knowledge of God, sang a song as though singing of the present day:
“God of hosts, turn us back, and show your face, and we shall be saved.”
The King of glory had not yet come, and the forerunners were proclaiming the kingdom. “You who shepherd Israel,” he said.
Speak clearly, prophet; explain what you are saying and proclaiming. For many have been shepherds:
Moses was a shepherd, Aaron was a shepherd:
For, he says, “He shepherded his people by the hand of Moses and Aaron.” David too was a shepherd: for, he says, “He chose David his servant to shepherd Israel, his inheritance.”
Why, then, do you conceal his dignity under the name of shepherd?
Make the distinction clear. With sound judgment and without confusion, receive the voice of the proclamation. He says: “You who shepherd Israel, give ear, you who lead Joseph like a sheep.”
By calling him a shepherd here, he does not yet make clear the dignity of the one proclaimed, because he shares this name with other shepherds.
What then? Have you still not understood his dignity? I will make the truth clear to you.
“You who sit upon the cherubim, reveal yourself; stir up your power and come to save us.” Do you see how he has fully disclosed the dignity of the one foretold?
Do you see how, by the royal throne above the world, he proclaimed Jesus as the King of glory?
Therefore the Savior too, confirming the name given by the prophet, cried out through the grace of the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd.”
For he said: “Since you did not recognize God as rational beings, at least recognize the shepherd as irrational sheep.”
The prophet, wishing to show the fruit of the Shepherd’s coming, said, “Stir up your strength and come to save us.”
For the Savior’s appearing is the source of every blessing. The Redeemer of the world therefore appeared, taking everything upon himself in accordance with the goodness proper to him.
Since he saw that everyone had fallen away from heavenly things, he himself renews in himself all his excellent gifts: the priesthood that he gave to Israel and prophecy.
And how? Listen.

He becomes a prophet, because prophecy had been corrupted by unworthy people, as it is written: “The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me.” He becomes an apostle and high priest, according to the saying:
“Consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of your calling.”
He becomes a priest, as the psalmist said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

He becomes a brother and a servant, as the valiant Paul said: “So that he might be the firstborn among many brothers”; and again he said, “For I say that Christ became a servant to the circumcised, to fulfill the promises made to the fathers.”
Thus he comes in every rank, and he also becomes a reader:
For he took Isaiah and read, as the Gospel relates, both to confirm the words of the prophets and to honor the church’s places of worship.
He also became King of kings, as Nathanael said: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.”
But perhaps someone standing here will say, “What does it matter to me, a layman, if he clothed himself in prophecy, apostleship, and the high priesthood?
What does it matter to me, who am numbered among the laity?” Rather, he who loves humanity became a human being for all humanity.
But if you wish to see him also taking the rank of a layman for your sake, consider within yourself and pay attention to what is about to be said.
It is acknowledged: is not the one who baptizes on the side of the priest, and is not the one being baptized in the rank of a layman?
Look, then, at John baptizing in the rank of a priest, and at Christ being baptized in the rank of a layman.
For today, brothers, today he fulfilled his saving plan through water, not being sanctified by the water, but giving sanctification to the water.
And John fulfilled the priestly role. The Redeemer of the world, who baptizes in the Spirit, approaches John, who baptizes in water: the King approaches the Forerunner, God approaches the prophet.
He did not fail to understand the dignity of the saving plan, nor did the bodily appearance confuse him.
Nor was he misled about the invisible power behind the visible appearance [?], which he proclaimed even to those who did not know it.
For the holy man was a lamp, a wonderful lamp, about whom it was said through the prophet: “I have prepared a lamp for my Anointed One.”
John was called a lamp beforehand, not because the Word of God, the true light, needed additional light from a lamp:
For he was the Sun of Righteousness, but because John recognized the Lord hidden in the flesh, as though in the night of the Jewish order,
shining forth the light of the divine Word. He is fittingly called a lamp.
And behold the wonder, brothers.
When the Master who came to us entered upon his work in the flesh, becoming human out of love for humanity, there was a strange wonder: God among human beings, the Master among servants,
the Creator among his creatures, the one who sanctifies among those being sanctified. Then John proclaimed his dignity, and a glorious and awesome wonder could be seen:
a lamp receiving the Sun of righteousness,
for a human being in need of redemption baptized the Lord, the Redeemer of all, not presumptuously taking this upon himself, but submitting to a command.
For then, at that moment, two prophetic voices came together:

the voice of one crying in the wilderness and the voice upon the waters. The true herald cries out, and the God of glory thunders. And there was the Trinity, worthy of worship, shining forth its glory:
the Father proclaiming the Son from above, the Son below carrying out the divine plan, and the Holy Spirit setting his seal upon the divine mystery.
And as the Father bore witness from above to his Only-begotten Son, the voice became so mighty that the heavens were torn apart:
for as Jesus came up from the water, the heavens were torn apart. They could not withstand the voice of such a testimony, awestruck at the divine plan.
But see this wonder: this voice tore apart the heavens, yet did not frighten the heretics.
“This is my beloved Son. Listen to him.”

Since the Law had preached beforehand and the prophets had proclaimed the good news, the divine voice distinguishes what is equal [?] from the Master's dignity, so that no one, held by the first arrangement of the Jewish order, might shake off the yoke of the grace of the Gospel.
"Hear him." Hear him who is plainly the Christ. For Christ is the fulfilment of the Law, and Jesus is the fulfilment of good things.
For although the blessings of the Law came first, they were not complete, awaiting our Lord, of whom the wonderful Paul said, “For Christ is the fulfillment of the Law.”
And if you wish, I will plainly set the truth before you through the events themselves, bearing witness to what has been said. Pay close attention.
Moses the lawgiver commanded the twelve tribes of Israel to divide, and he brought six tribes up onto Mount Ebal,
and six onto Mount Gerizim. He commanded the one group to bless and the other to curse:
to bless those who kept the Law and to curse those who transgressed it. What, then?
With the curses, the confirming seal of everyone was added. For he said, “The Levites shall say, ‘Cursed is anyone who abandons the Law of the Lord God.’”
And all the people shall say, “Amen.” And at each commandment the same “Amen” was added to the curse upon those who transgressed.

But concerning the blessing, the Levites shall say, “Blessed is the one who keeps the Law of the Lord; blessed in the field, blessed in the city, blessed in battle.” Yet there is no “Amen” at any one of the blessings.
Why, then, do the curses receive confirmation, while the blessings receive no seal?

What, then, does this arrangement mean? What does this mystery signify? As far as I am able, I will strive to explain it, given wings by your love. The Law fulfilled the pronouncement of the curse, but Jesus confirmed the good tidings. The blessings remained incomplete,

because it was fitting that what belonged to the Law should be given through the Law, while what belonged to the grace of the gospel should be held in reserve. For this reason the blessings remained, still awaiting the addition of the word “Amen.”
And so that no one may suppose the statement to be forced by grace, but rather attested by the truth itself, listen to the most wise Paul, who says:
Our Lord and God Jesus Christ was not both “Yes” and “No”; rather, everything in him became “Yes.”
For all God's promises in him are “Yes,” and likewise “Amen,” to the glory of God.
From this we can understand what the apostle himself said: “When we were dead through our transgressions and the uncircumcision of our flesh,
he made us alive together with himself, forgiving us all our transgressions and erasing the written bond against us.”

Since every written bond is confirmed through the [?] of the legal scribe and by the borrower's signature, it is necessary to know when, where, and how it was made. It therefore has the grounds mentioned above here: the law pronounced curses, while the people listening signed their assent with “Amen.”
Jesus was the fulfillment of blessings, appearing at the Jordan and fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy.
For Isaiah said: “Let the wilderness of the Jordan rejoice, for the glory of Lebanon and the honor of Carmel have been given to it.” The saying is not clear, but it will become clear by God's grace.
Here Scripture calls Jerusalem “Lebanon,” and do not think this is a forced interpretation. Ezekiel bears witness concerning King Nebuchadnezzar, saying:
“A great eagle, with great wings, its wings outstretched and full of talons, came to Babylon,
and took the choicest parts of the cedar of Lebanon and carried them away to Babylon.” And what were these choicest parts? For he bound King Zedekiah, Jehoiakim, the priests, and the high priest:
these were the choicest parts of Lebanon, and he carried them away to Babylon. So here too it was said that the glory of Lebanon had been given to it.
For both the priesthood of Jerusalem and all prophecy passed to John, and all Jerusalem left the altar and went out to receive John's baptism.
And the prophet, speaking beforehand about the wilderness of the Jordan, says that the glory of Lebanon and the honor of Carmel have been given to it.
And what honor? Listen as I explain it in passing. Elijah was the honor of Carmel, for the prophet Elijah lived on Carmel.

Since John went before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, consider this saying: “The honor of Carmel has been given to the wilderness.” For John was a new Elijah in the wilderness, about whom the Savior said: “If you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come.”
Since Elijah once lived in the wilderness, and now John does, he fittingly said: “The glory of Lebanon and the honor of Carmel have been given to it.”
Now, beloved, that glory has filled not only the wilderness but the whole inhabited world, for today there are songs and praises of God throughout the earth.
From evening until now people have stood, and with their songs they have surpassed song; grace was displayed, and human nature was not apparent.
And most fittingly so. For when iron is joined with fire, what it was is no longer visible,

and it clothes itself in what it was not, without casting off its nature, but receiving brightness within its nature. So we too, having been granted the Holy Spirit, have cast off bodily weakness and clothed ourselves in the working of grace.
The church stood shining throughout the night, and in it the saying is fulfilled: “There was evening, and there was morning, a day.” The night had no darkness:

For it was illuminated by the divine word, as David said: “And the night is light for my food, for darkness will not be dark before you, and the night will shine like the day.” For such great beauty lights up the Church and shines upon it like a splendid crown, worthy of the crown of the kingdom that God will give to the whole world.

From a good root a good branch has blossomed. When I say this, I am singing of the pair of brothers and the harmony of their reign. The divine word is indeed true: "A brother helped by a brother is like a strong city and like a firmly established kingdom." These are the two rich olive trees that stand before the Lord of all the earth. They are flowers of piety and pillars of truth, and they shelter the Church, since Christ also shelters their kingdom. I see the branches together with the root, the blessed king, shining with his children. For the glory of the righteous has not died, since "the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance." Do you see them shining with his image? It is not a lifeless image but a living one. I look at what has gone before and I am amazed: how did [?] the terrors of war all scatter?

The faith of that faithful great king, their father, shelters the children of the kingdom. God, who led that king, also leads his offspring, who have sprung from a fruitful root. Let us pray, brethren, that they may be preserved: the lamps of Christian good order, the olive branches, the two lamps of piety, the shelter of the Church. Let no one think these words are flattery. They are true facts. "What?" someone says. "Does a man shelter the Church?" Very much so. Do you not know that God, who gives great things to men, asks small things from us? He gave manna in the wilderness, and he asks the priests for loaves, saying: "Set loaves on the table before me." He gave a pillar of fire, and he said: "Set a lampstand before me." He grants so great a source of light, and he borrows a lampstand, so that by what I give I may show abundance, and by what you ask of me [?] you may fulfil thanksgiving. The Church also shines again, first of all with the holy fathers.

But we must keep the length of the discourse in view, and the one who sets the measure of a discourse is not the speaker but the listener. Since your words have been exhausted [?] by untiring zeal, I must measure the discourse, bring it to a close here, and be sanctified by divine grace. The Holy Trinity enlightens us, together with the presiding of the fathers and the wealth of the whole Church. It is like a flowered, richly coloured garment of the Church that catches the sun's ray and makes the walls, the roofs and the people standing there shine. Whatever the beauty of the colour, such is the colouring it produces in the air, whether gilded, green or purple, or adorned with any colour the dyer's art can produce. In the same way the Church sometimes receives the rays of prophecy, and at other times the working of the grace of the Gospel, so that she stands [?] as the prophetic voice says, shining in many-coloured garments, according to what was said:

The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold-embroidered garments and richly adorned. Why does it say “stood”? So that Paul may speak truly when he says, “He presented the Church to himself in glory, without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind.” May we too, brothers, always sanctified by divine grace, offer glory to the all-holy God, for to him belong all glory, honor, dominion, and majesty, forever and ever. Amen.
